reasoning: The study generates original research data: it recruits and scans 8 svPPA patients and controls with 11C-PBR28 and 18F-flortaucipir PET, acquires MRI, neuropsychological, and neuropathological data specifically for this study, classifying it as Data Generated (D1). For software, the paper only uses existing established tools (FreeSurfer, PMOD, SPM12, IBM SPSS, MATLAB curve fitting toolbox) for processing and statistical analysis, without claiming to develop or significantly extend any software, so this is Software Used (S2).

The paper reports an original spectroscopic host-galaxy redshift survey (3147 new redshifts, plus SNANA simulation libraries and adjusted CC SN luminosity function templates) — this constitutes newly generated research data (D1). It also describes the authors' own implementation of the BEAMS method, which they explicitly state is new code available on GitHub ("Our code is available online," github.com/djones1040/BEAMS), going beyond mere use of existing tools like SNANA/emcee — this is research software generated (S1), with the general rule that generated implies used as well.

The paper reports an original experiment generating new research data: PTPRC genotyping results, erythrocyte/leukocyte profiles, PBMC proliferation assays, and IgG ELISA data from a cattle tick infestation trial. This constitutes data generation (D1). For software, the authors only used standard/generic statistical tools (R, the mgcv and jtrans packages, gam.check) for data analysis — these are generic statistical software, not research software created or substantially extended by the authors, and software is not claimed as a contribution. No bespoke software or scripts are described as being developed. Hence this falls under S3 (No Research Software) and D1 (Research Data Generated).

This is a theoretical/conceptual paper that reviews literature on bureaucracy and Weber's theory, then maps nine bureaucracy concepts onto features of the Balanced Scorecard framework based on existing published sources (Kaplan & Norton's work). It explicitly states 'this paper does not offer empirical support for the arguments made' and proposes future case study research instead. No research data (no collected/generated recorded information, measurements, or derived statistics) and no research software are created or used anywhere in the paper.

This is a literature review paper summarizing existing studies on energy storage technologies for renewable-energy-driven water desalination systems. It does not generate or use its own research software (the "simulations" mentioned are from cited third-party studies, not conducted by this paper's authors) nor does it collect, generate, or analyze its own research data—it only synthesizes findings reported in other papers. The explicit "Data Availability Statement: Not applicable" further confirms no data was generated or used by the authors themselves.

The paper uses existing machine learning software (Weka and JADBio) to analyze data—no new software/source code is created or significantly extended, so it is S2 (software used). Regarding data, while the primary 192-patient autism assessment dataset is reused from a prior publication, the paper also designs and administers two novel screening questionnaires (ASTA tools) to new cohorts of patients (30 and 18 patients respectively), collecting new survey/assessment data specifically for this research. This newly collected data constitutes generated research data, placing the paper in D1 per the rule that generating data implies the generated category even if existing data is also used."

The paper develops a novel hierarchical EMS (MILP optimization, ANFIS forecasting, adaptive AR forecasting, and a real-time predictive rule-based controller) implemented as custom scripts/algorithms in MATLAB and LABVIEW specifically for this research—this is research software generated (the control/optimization logic itself is a core research contribution, not merely a utility like plotting software). The paper also generates research data: experimental measurements from a real laboratory microgrid (power drawn, SOC, load/PV profiles collected via CANBUS during the real-time experiment) and simulation outputs across seasons, plus synthetic load profiles created via the CREST model for this specific MG scenario. Since data and software are both generated (and used), per the general rule the paper falls into the generated categories for both dimensions.

The study collected original raw field recordings and 360° videos, created new experimental soundscape samples, and gathered new survey/questionnaire data (SQE, LoW responses, demographics) from 120 participants in Peace Gardens, Sheffield — this constitutes generated research data (D1), including deposit on Mendeley Data. For software, the paper only mentions use of generic tools (SPSS for statistics, Matlab for clustering, Adobe Audition for audio editing) as utilities for processing/analysis, not as a research contribution, and no custom software or scripts were created or significantly extended. Hence no research software is claimed (S3).

The study generated new behavioral observation data (CCTV-based ethogram recordings of binturong activity) during zoo open/closed conditions, which counts as research data generated (D1). No research software was created or used as a contribution; the paper only used generic/widely-established tools (R statistical software for analysis, Microsoft Excel for data entry), which are excluded as research software under the criteria, and no other software is claimed as a contribution — hence S3.

The paper reports a post-hoc analysis of the SSaSS cluster-randomised trial, where the authors generated new research data by collecting and recording fatal/non-fatal cancer events through face-to-face follow-up, hospitalisation record linkage, and mortality surveillance over 4.7 years—this constitutes research data generation (D1). No research software was created or used beyond SAS version 9.4, a generic statistical software package explicitly excluded from the research software definition, so this is classified as S3 (No Research Software).

The study acquired and analyzed original EEG-fMRI, structural MRI, and clinical data from a cohort of 10 epilepsy patients, constituting newly generated research data (D1). For analysis, the authors used existing established research software tools (SPM12/DCM10, FSL, Freesurfer, 3D Slicer, ICN_Atlas, SEEGA) without claiming to have created or significantly extended any of these tools themselves, placing software use in S2.

This is a narrative review article that discusses and synthesizes findings from previously published GWAS and Mendelian randomisation studies on the genetic relationship between type 2 diabetes and cancer. The authors did not conduct original data collection/analysis, did not generate or significantly extend any research data themselves, and did not create or use any research software as part of the reported work (literature review and discussion only). Per the criteria, literature/papers are explicitly excluded from being considered research data, and there is no evidence of software use or creation by the authors in producing this review.

The paper develops a conceptual "agile model" (a methodology/framework combining lean, smart, and green manufacturing concepts) rather than any software tool — no source code, scripts, or model implementation is claimed as a contribution (a suggestion to "design software" for path planning is a future recommendation to industry, not software created or used by the researchers), so S3. The authors collected new empirical data through Gemba walks, brainstorming sessions, interviews, and direct measurements on two real production shop floors (automobile and mining machinery plants), reported as observed production conditions and before/after performance metrics (Tables 2–5). This is data generated through the research's own fieldwork/observation, meeting the D1 (Research Data Generated) definition.

The paper is an empirical economics study using the pre-existing Russian Longitudinal Monitoring Survey (RLMS), a panel survey not created by the authors—so research data is used, not generated. The authors apply standard fixed-effects and ordered logit regressions (likely via generic statistical software) without claiming to create or extend any research software, so no research software is involved (S3).

The paper is a pure mathematics (linear algebra) paper proving theorems about matrix symmetry decompositions and pseudoinverses. It does not claim to create or use any research software (any numerical computation, e.g., SVD/Smith normal form of the Wilson matrix, is illustrative mathematics, not a software contribution or tool usage described as part of the methodology). It explicitly states "No data was used for the research described in the article," and the Wilson matrix example is a standard textbook test matrix used purely as a worked illustration, not research data generated or used per the UKRI definition. Hence S3 (no software) and D3 (no data).

The paper uses an existing numerical rotating-convection model (code described in Willis et al. 2007), run and analyzed by the authors but not claimed to be newly created or significantly extended in this paper—this is S2 (software used). Plotting tools (VisIt, Matplotlib, seaborn) are mere utilities, not research software contributions. The paper generates substantial new research data via its suite of 68+ numerical simulations (temperature/velocity fields, thermal gradient profiles, etc.), which qualifies as D1 (data generated), even though the paper states the data is only "available on request."

The authors analyzed a pre-existing publicly available dataset (NABEC long-read sequencing/structural variant data, dbGaP phs001300), which they explicitly state was "publicly available datasets...analyzed in this study" and provided by colleagues rather than generated by this research (D2 - Data Used). For software, they relied entirely on existing third-party research tools (Napu pipeline, Sniffles2, EMBOSS/Transeq, FASTA, BLAST, RepeatMasker, MAFFT, IQ-TREE2, RIdeogram, Figtree) with default parameters, with no claim of creating or significantly extending any software (S2 - Software Used).

The paper uses existing surveillance/traveler data (WHO case reports, traveler volume statistics, length-of-stay data) to derive case estimates via a mathematical formula and profile-likelihood CIs; no new primary dataset is created, only statistics/estimates derived from existing sources, which falls under D2 (data used). There is no mention of any research software (code, scripts, models) being created or used beyond standard statistical calculations, so it is S3 (no research software).

The paper reports original fieldwork/laboratory observations (shark collection, copepod dissection, histological sectioning and staining) generating new research data (histopathology observations, infection prevalence/intensity measurements). No research software is mentioned anywhere—only generic lab equipment (autostainer) and physical preparation methods are used, with no claim of creating or using any software tool.

The paper isolates and sequences 44 new flavobacterial phages, generating new genomic sequence data, TEM morphology data, and metagenome-derived abundance data, which were deposited in NCBI (PRJNA639310) — clear research data generation (D1). For analysis, the authors exclusively use existing, previously published research software tools (SPAdes, Tadpole, Bandage, PhageTerm, VirClust, ViPTree, VICTOR, VIRIDIC, MUSCLE, IQ-Tree, BLASTN, WIsH, CRISPRCasFinder, Geneious, ARB, RAxML, MiGA, FigTree, GRAViTy) and a previously described custom annotation/read-mapping pipeline ("described elsewhere"), with no claim of creating or substantially extending new software themselves (S2).

The paper runs an extensive Monte Carlo simulation study, generating synthetic data under various model misspecifications (local dependence, nonnormal latent distributions) to evaluate the LM tests — this constitutes generated research data (simulation inputs/outputs), which per the rules takes precedence even though they also use an existing real dataset (Detroit Area Study) for the applied example. On the software side, the authors use existing tools (R's "optim" function, the "NumDeriv" and "ltm" R packages) to perform estimation and numerical derivatives, but do not claim to have created or significantly extended any software package themselves — so this is software used (S2), not generated.

The paper presents the creation of the Cool Farm Biodiversity metric, an online research software tool built and co-owned by the authors (CRediT statement lists "Software" contributions; software/data availability statement describes the tool as managed/co-owned by the authors' institutions), clearly qualifying as S1 (Software Generated). The paper also reports generation of new research data through structured expert elicitation and modified Delphi processes (judgement and evidence scores for actions/species groups across biomes, provided in Supplementary Table S12), as well as farm management example data used to demonstrate the metric's responsiveness — this constitutes D1 (Data Generated).

The paper generates new experimental data: solid dispersions of ibuprofen with various polymers were prepared and characterized via PXRD, DSC, FTIR spectroscopy, and dissolution studies, producing original research data (D1). No research software is created or substantively used as a research contribution; the software mentioned (EVA for PXRD, TA Universal Analysis for DSC, OMNIC for FTIR) are generic commercial instrument/data-processing tools used only as utilities for analyzing data, not research software developed or significantly extended by the authors, so this is S3.

This is a humanities/architectural history article that relies on archival research (letters, exhibition catalogues, RIBA records) and secondary literature to construct a historical narrative about Oliver Hill's exhibition design. No research software is created or used (no tools, code, or computational methods are mentioned). The archival sources function as historical/textual evidence akin to literature and documentary records rather than research data generated or systematically collected/analyzed per the UKRI definition—there is no dataset creation, measurement, or structured data collection/analysis, just close reading and historical argumentation. Hence S3D3.

This is a scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) that systematically searched databases and extracted/synthesized findings from 7 previously published clinical studies. No research software was created or used beyond generic utilities (EndNote for duplicate removal, Excel worksheet for recording) which are explicitly excluded as "not research software" (S3). The paper uses existing published research (data) to derive findings and synthesize results, but does not generate any new research data of its own (D2).

The paper reports a new crystal structure determination (synthesis, X-ray diffraction, refinement) producing novel research data (atomic coordinates, displacement parameters, bond lengths/angles, hydrogen-bond geometry, CCDC deposit 1537099), so D1 applies. All software used (APEX3, SAINT, SADABS, SHELXT, SHELXL, DIAMOND) are pre-existing third-party crystallographic programs used as utilities for data collection/structure solution/refinement/visualization; there is no claim of creating or extending software, so S3 applies.

The paper reports original research data generated through seven interviews/focus groups (22 teachers) and a follow-up survey of 25 former lead schools, which were collected specifically for this project evaluation — qualifying as generated research data (D1). The only software mentioned is NVivo, a generic qualitative data analysis package used merely as a utility for coding/clustering transcripts, not developed or significantly extended as a research contribution, so this falls under S3 (no research software) per the criteria's explicit exclusion of generic data processing tools used as utilities.

This is a review article surveying published literature on protein–ionic liquid interactions (solubility data, simulations, reaction studies). The authors do not report generating or using their own research software or research data; all tables, simulation results, and solubility figures are drawn from and attributed to prior published studies, which are literature/citations rather than data or software produced or used by this paper's own research. No methods, datasets, or software tools are claimed as the authors' contribution.

This is a qualitative, interpretive case study of Ach. Brito, built on primary empirical material the authors collected themselves: 25 personal interviews, non-participant observations, and archival/document research conducted over 2007–2014. This constitutes newly generated research data (D1). There is no mention of any research software being created or used (beyond generic qualitative content analysis as a method, not a tool), so the paper is S3 for software.

The paper reports original experimental data (PL spectra, ODMR spectra, g2(τ) intensity-correlation measurements, angle-dependent measurements) generated through the authors' own confocal microscopy and ODMR experiments on hBN defects—clear D1. Regarding software, the "Code availability" statement only refers to generic analysis code used for curve-fitting (bi-/tri-exponential, Lorentzian fits) and simulations, which function as data-processing utilities rather than a research software contribution in their own right; there is no claim of developing or significantly extending research software, so this is S3.
